title: Buckets: S3 for runs

story: At step 4 of the build for RH-1234, Nova's VM freezes. Five minutes later the workflow declares it dead and claims a fresh one. Everything on the old disk is gone, and yet Nova continues from where it was, with its whole conversation intact, because while it worked, the harness, our program on the VM that runs Nova, had been saving the session transcript to S3, AWS's storage service for files.

That raises a puzzle. The VM holds no AWS keys and its role cannot touch S3, on purpose. Still, the harness wrote dozens of files into a private, encrypted bucket. Something let it write exactly those files, and nothing else.
hook.question: How can a machine with no AWS credentials save files to S3, and only the files it is meant to save?

p: S3 stores objects in buckets. A bucket is a named container, and its name is unique across all of AWS, which is why ours is called rhino-ai-agents-runs and not just runs. An object is a file's bytes plus a key, its name. A key such as runs/nova-RH-1234/sessions/part-0001.jsonl looks like a path, but S3 has no real folders: runs/nova-RH-1234/ is only a prefix, the start shared by many keys. That makes prefixes the natural unit for permissions, because "everything this run wrote" is simply "every key that starts with runs/nova-RH-1234/".

Each run writes under its own prefix: notes, a small checkpoint record, and the session transcript, one part per write, under sessions/. When a run continues on a fresh VM, the harness lists its own prefix and reads the parts back in order.

code.file: your terminal, pointed at the practice AWS
code.text:
aws s3 cp notes.md s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/nova-RH-1234/notes.md
aws s3 ls s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/nova-RH-1234/ --recursive

notes.text: --recursive lists every key under the prefix, as if the prefix were a folder.

read.h: A link that carries its own permission
p: The answer to the puzzle is a presigned URL. Normally every request to S3 is signed with the caller's credentials, and S3 checks the signature and the caller's policies. A presigned URL is that same signed request, prepared in advance by someone who does have permission, and handed to someone who does not. It names one operation (PUT or GET), one bucket and one key, and an expiry. Whoever holds the URL can make exactly that request, with no credentials of their own, until it expires.

In the platform, the one who signs is the broker, the service that holds every credential the VM must not have. When the harness wants to save a transcript part, it asks the broker for a link. The broker checks that the name is clean and falls under this run's prefix, then signs a PUT for that one key, valid for 15 minutes, with its own role. The harness uploads with a plain fetch. The code below is the signing part, the same call the broker makes, outside the broker.

notes.text: Credentials come from the environment, as they do for the broker's role. forcePathStyle puts the bucket in the path, which LocalStack needs.
The request being signed: one command, one bucket, one key.
Seconds until the link dies. The broker uses 900, 15 minutes; S3 refuses anything over 7 days.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what is inside the link
p: Split a presigned URL at ? and & and you can read it. X-Amz-Credential names the signer's access key ID, the date, the region and the service, but never the secret. X-Amz-Expires is the lifetime in seconds. X-Amz-Signature is a hash computed with the signer's secret over the method, the path and these parameters. S3 recomputes it on every request, so changing the key or the expiry by one character makes the signature wrong, and the answer is 403.
If a link leaks into a log, the damage is one object for at most 15 minutes. That is the reason for short lifetimes: a link is a bearer token, and anyone who holds it can use it.

read.h: Three refusals that make it safe
p: Follow one link through its life and you meet three checks. The broker refuses to sign anything outside the run's own prefix, so the harness cannot ask for another run's files. S3 refuses a link that was changed after signing, so the harness cannot turn part-0001 into part-0002, or the PUT into a DELETE. And S3 refuses a link after its expiry, with "Request has expired". None of these checks depends on the VM behaving well, which is the point: a fooled agent holds a few links that each open one object for a few minutes.

read.h: Private, encrypted, and gone after 30 days
p: The bucket itself is configured so that a mistake in a policy can never make it public, and nothing in it lives forever. Block Public Access is four switches that override any policy or old per-object setting that would make data public; all four are on. Default encryption uses SSE-KMS, server-side encryption with a key from KMS (the AWS key service) that belongs to this bucket, so every object is encrypted at rest without the writer doing anything; the bucket key setting makes S3 ask KMS less often, which keeps costs down. Versioning keeps the old version when an object is overwritten or deleted, so one bad write does not destroy a run's work.

A lifecycle rule tells S3 to act on objects by age, and the runs bucket deletes everything under runs/ after 30 days. The harness's session store, the code that writes the transcript parts, never deletes anything itself, so this rule is the only thing that removes old runs. With versioning on, an expired object only gets a delete marker and its old version stays, so a second action removes old versions after a day. Once the rule is in place, S3 tells you the planned deletion date of every object it covers, as the line under the code shows.

notes.text: Only keys that start with runs/. A typo here and nothing ever expires.
30 days after it was written, the current version of an object is deleted.
Old versions, kept by versioning, are removed one day after they stop being current.

lab.title: A runs bucket and links with no keys
needs: AWS CLI v2 and the LocalStack image from the p3-1 lab
lab.goal: Upload a transcript part through a presigned URL from a shell with no AWS credentials, watch S3 refuse a changed link and an expired one, then protect the bucket the way the platform does.

guess.q: The broker signs a PUT link for runs/nova-RH-1234/sessions/part-0001.jsonl, valid for 15 minutes. A fooled harness edits the link to point at part-0002.jsonl and uses it at once. What happens?

options.text: It works, because the link is still within its 15 minutes.
options.why: Time is only one of the checks. The key is part of what was signed, so the edited link no longer matches its signature.

options.text: It works, but only inside the run's own prefix.
options.why: S3 does not know about runs or prefixes here. It only knows that this exact request was not the one that was signed.

options.text: S3 answers 403, because the signature no longer matches the request.
options.why: The signature covers the method, the bucket, the key and the expiry. Change any of them and S3 refuses the request.

follow.say: LocalStack skips signature checks by default, so start it with real checks turned on. If it is running from an earlier lab, remove it first with docker rm -f localstack.
follow.do: docker run --rm -d --name localstack -e S3_SKIP_SIGNATURE_VALIDATION=0 -p 4566:4566 localstack/localstack:4.9 && sleep 15

follow.say: Create the runs bucket and save one note under the run's prefix, the normal way, with credentials.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p3-6 && cd ~/academy-labs/p3-6 && export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs
echo "plan v2 approved by Sean" > notes.md && aws s3 cp notes.md s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/nova-RH-1234/notes.md

follow.say: Install the AWS SDK for JavaScript and save the signing script from Understand. This terminal plays the broker: it has credentials and signs links.
follow.do:
npm init -y > /dev/null && npm pkg set type=module && npm i @aws-sdk/client-s3@3.700.0 @aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner@3.700.0
Save presign.mjs from Understand.
follow.see: added 105 packages, and audited 106 packages in 20s

X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD

follow.say: Now play the VM: upload with curl in a shell that has no AWS credentials at all. env -u removes the two variables for this one command.
follow.do:
echo '{"type":"user","text":"Add the No projects yet card"}' > part-0001.jsonl
env -u AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID -u AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'upload: HTTP %{http_code}\n' -X PUT --upload-file part-0001.jsonl "$PUT"
aws s3 ls s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/nova-RH-1234/ --recursive

follow.say: Be the fooled harness: point the same link at another key.
Sign a GET that lives 5 seconds, use it, wait, and use it again.
follow.do: GET=$(node presign.mjs GET runs/nova-RH-1234/sessions/part-0001.jsonl 5) && curl -s "$GET" && sleep 7 && curl -s "$GET" | grep -o '<Message>[^<]*</Message>'
follow.see:
{"type":"user","text":"Add the No projects yet card"}
<Message>Request has expired</Message>

lab.build: Make the bucket match the platform's. Create a KMS key (aws kms create-key --description "runs bucket" --query KeyMetadata.Arn --output text), set default encryption to aws:kms with that key and BucketKeyEnabled true (put-bucket-encryption), turn on all four Block Public Access switches (put-public-access-block), turn on versioning (put-bucket-versioning), and add the 30-day rule from Understand (put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration). Upload notes.md again, then prove it all with head-object: the object must report aws:kms with the bucket key, and an expiry date 30 days away.
checks: The upload through the presigned URL prints HTTP 200 from a shell with no AWS credentials, and the part shows up in aws s3 ls.
The link edited to part-0002 prints HTTP 403.
The 5-second GET works once, then answers Request has expired.
head-object on notes.md shows aws:kms and True, and an expiry-date about 30 days ahead with rule-id expire-runs-after-30-days.
get-bucket-versioning prints Enabled, and get-public-access-block shows four True values.

solution.text:
KEY=$(aws kms create-key --description "runs bucket" --query KeyMetadata.Arn --output text)
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs --server-side-encryption-configuration \
  "{\"Rules\":[{\"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault\":{\"SSEAlgorithm\":\"aws:kms\",\"KMSMasterKeyID\":\"$KEY\"},\"BucketKeyEnabled\":true}]}"
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs --public-access-block-configuration \
  BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json

aws s3 cp notes.md s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/nova-RH-1234/notes.md --quiet
aws s3api head-object --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs --key runs/nova-RH-1234/notes.md \
  --query '[ServerSideEncryption, BucketKeyEnabled, Expiration]' --output text
# aws:kms  True  expiry-date="Sun, 15 Nov 2026 00:00:00 GMT", rule-id="expire-runs-after-30-days"

lab.fix: Uploads failed a few times on a slow network, so a teammate changed the default in presign.mjs from "900" to "604800", seven days, the most S3 allows. Make the change, sign a PUT, and read X-Amz-Expires in the link with tr as in step 4. Then think it through: links often land in places like debug logs and error reports, which are often kept for longer than a week. Put the default back to 900, and write one sentence on what a slow upload should do instead of using a week-long link.
explain: The VM holds no AWS credentials. Why can it still upload a transcript part, and why only that one part?
Which three checks does a link meet, and which of them are done by S3 itself?
Why does the runs bucket need both Expiration and NoncurrentVersionExpiration?
lab.done: An upload with no credentials works through a 15-minute link, edited and expired links get 403, and the bucket is encrypted, private, versioned and set to expire run files after 30 days.

check.q: What does a presigned PUT URL from the broker allow its holder to do?

options.text: Upload anything under the run's prefix for 15 minutes
options.why: The signature covers one exact key. Prefixes only matter to the broker when it decides whether to sign.

options.text: Upload one object at one exact key until the link expires
options.why: Method, bucket, key and expiry are all part of the signature, so the link opens exactly one door for a short time.

options.text: Act as the broker's role in S3 until the link expires
options.why: The link carries no credentials, only a signature for one request. The secret never leaves the broker.

check.q: A presigned link leaks into a public log. What is the worst case with our settings?

options.text: Someone can do that link's one operation, a read or a write, on that one object for at most 15 minutes
options.why: That is why the lifetime is short and each link names one key.

options.text: Someone can list and download the whole runs bucket
options.why: Listing is a different request that was never signed. The link is good for one operation on one key.

options.text: Nothing, because a link only works from inside our VPC
options.why: A presigned URL works for anyone who holds it, wherever they are. That is why its lifetime must be short.

check.q: Versioning is on, and the lifecycle rule has only Expiration after 30 days. What happens to a transcript part on day 31?

options.why: With versioning on, expiration only adds a delete marker. The data stays as an old version.

options.text: Nothing, because lifecycle rules do not work with versioning
options.why: They work, but expiring the current version is only half of the job.

options.text: It gets a delete marker and its data stays as an old version, until a NoncurrentVersionExpiration action removes it
options.why: That is why the rule needs both actions: one for current objects and one for the old versions that versioning keeps.

p: The runs bucket, rhino-ai-agents-runs, lives in the ai-agents account with its own KMS key, all public access blocked, versioning on and a 30-day expiry, and the S3 endpoint in the sandbox VPC allows only our buckets. The broker's role may put and get objects under runs/* and nothing else, and it is the only identity that signs links.

The broker's artifacts API returns a 15-minute presigned PUT or GET for s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/<run_id>/<name>, after cleaning the name, and lists a run's own objects so a resumed run can find its parts. The harness's session store writes every transcript batch through those links, which is how a run continues on a fresh VM after a crash, a question or a lost Spot machine.

tickets.why: Creates the runs bucket with its own KMS key, Block Public Access, versioning and the 30-day expiry.
The broker's artifacts API: 15-minute presigned links for the run's own prefix only.
The session store that mirrors every transcript batch to S3 through those links.
The broker's role, allowed to put and get objects under runs/* only.

words.plain: An object's full name, like runs/nova-RH-1234/notes.md; a prefix is the start shared by many keys, not a real folder.
A request signed in advance for one operation on one object, usable by anyone who holds it until it expires.
Server-side encryption with a KMS key: S3 encrypts every object at rest with a key you control.
Four bucket switches that override any setting that would make data public.
A bucket rule that acts on objects by age, such as deleting runs/ objects after 30 days.

review.q: Describe, step by step, how a transcript part gets from the harness into S3.
review.a: The harness asks the broker for a link for runs/<run_id>/sessions/<part>; the broker checks the name and the run's prefix and signs a 15-minute PUT with its own role; the harness uploads with fetch; S3 checks the signature and the expiry and stores the object, encrypted.

review.q: Name the bucket settings of rhino-ai-agents-runs and what each one protects against.
review.a: Block Public Access (a policy mistake making data public), SSE-KMS with its own key (data readable at rest), versioning (a bad overwrite or delete), and the 30-day lifecycle rule (transcripts kept forever).

review.q: Why does the broker sign links for 15 minutes and not for a week?
review.a: A link is a bearer token: anyone holding it can use it. A short lifetime limits the damage of a leak to one object for a few minutes; a slow upload should ask for a fresh link instead.

remember: A VM with no keys saves its work through links the broker signs: one object, one operation, 15 minutes, into a bucket that is private, encrypted and empties itself after 30 days.
